name: Gonadorelin

lead: Gonadorelin is lab-made GnRH, the brain signal that makes the pituitary release LH and FSH. On TRT forums it is used in place of hCG to keep the testes active, aiming for less testicular shrinkage and steadier hormones.

It binds GnRH receptors on the pituitary, triggering LH and FSH release. Doctors have used it for diagnostic testing and, as pulsed infusions, to restore ovulation or fertility in people with GnRH deficiency. No trial has compared it with hCG in men on testosterone, and users report mixed results.

paras: TRT users take it on a regular schedule alongside testosterone, as a substitute for hCG, often prescribed by clinics that offer TRT. Because it is cleared within minutes, how it is pulsed matters.

Documented trials are in specialist reproductive settings. In TRT use, reports are anecdotal, some users describe persistent atrophy, and continuous exposure desensitises receptors. Supply may come from clinics or compounding sources of varying regulation.

angle.text: Gonadorelin is synthetic GnRH that TRT users take in place of hCG to prompt LH and FSH release, keeping the testes active and limiting testicular shrinkage. It is established in fertility medicine and diagnostics; forum posters report mixed results in TRT.

lead: Gonadorelin is the synthetic form of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the hypothalamic decapeptide that prompts the pituitary to release luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) [1][2]. In medicine it has been used to test pituitary responsiveness and, delivered in pulses, to induce ovulation in women with hypothalamic amenorrhea and to restore fertility in people with GnRH deficiency [3][2].

In testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) and bodybuilding communities, gonadorelin is discussed as a substitute for hCG. Exogenous testosterone suppresses the brain's LH and FSH signal to the testes, and users want to keep that signal going so the testes stay full-sized and keep producing sperm and some of their own testosterone, which they see as part of a fuller, more masculine physique and appearance. Some clinics prescribe it for this purpose, and forum users report mixed experiences [4][5][6][7].

Published trials cover diagnostic and fertility uses in patients with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or amenorrhea [3][8][9]. No trial has compared gonadorelin with hCG in men on testosterone therapy, and none has examined appearance outcomes.
infobox: GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) agonist, identical in structure to native GnRH [2]
Injection, infusion by pump, or nasal spray; unstable when taken by mouth [19][2]
Distribution 2 to 10 minutes, terminal 10 to 40 minutes [2]
Prescription-only in Canada; Wikipedia states it is not available for clinical use in humans in the US [2]

paras: Gonadorelin has been used as a diagnostic stimulation test of the pituitary and to treat primary hypothalamic amenorrhea, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (including Kallmann syndrome), delayed puberty, cryptorchidism and infertility [1][2]. Unlike the long-acting GnRH analogues, it is not used to suppress sex hormones [2]. For treatment it is typically given as pulses from a portable pump, and it also exists as an intravenous or subcutaneous solution and a nasal spray [2].

A multicenter trial of pulsatile intravenous gonadorelin (Lutrepulse) in 109 women with hypothalamic amenorrhea reported ovulation in 91% and 96% of the primary and secondary amenorrhea groups [3]. Other registered studies have used pulsatile GnRH in men with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and in women with polycystic ovary syndrome [10][11]. It is also used in veterinary reproduction, particularly in dairy cattle protocols [12][13].

In appearance communities, the interest is in keeping the testes and hormone axis active during testosterone therapy. Users describe testicular size and fullness, fertility and avoiding the shrinkage that exogenous androgens can cause as the reasons for adding an LH-mimicking or GnRH-based agent [4][14][7]. This sits alongside other physique goals for which TRT and anabolic-androgen users run supporting medications.

GnRH, also called gonadoliberin or LHRH, is a decapeptide cut from a 92-amino-acid precursor and released in pulses by hypothalamic neurons into the portal blood that supplies the pituitary, where it prompts release of LH and FSH and so drives the testes or ovaries [15]. Pulse frequency and amplitude shape the LH and FSH output. It is cleared within minutes, which is why researchers often follow LH pulses as an indirect measure of its secretion [15].

The axis is active in fetal life and early infancy, quiet in childhood and reactivated at puberty. Kisspeptin stimulates GnRH release, and elevated prolactin can suppress pulsatile secretion; Kallmann syndrome is a congenital GnRH deficiency [15][16]. Roger Guillemin and Andrew Schally clarified the hormone's identity, work recognised by the 1977 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine [15].

Testosterone given from outside the body suppresses this natural LH and FSH signal, and Wikipedia notes that exogenous testosterone may suppress spermatogenesis and in some cases cause infertility [17]. hCG mimics LH and is used with testosterone replacement to help maintain fertility and prevent testicular atrophy [7]. Gonadorelin's rationale in forums is that it restores the upstream hypothalamic signal instead, so the pituitary keeps releasing LH and FSH [4][5].

Gonadorelin binds GnRH receptors on pituitary gonadotroph cells and triggers LH and FSH release. It has a distribution half-life of about 2 to 10 minutes and is broken down by hydrolysis into small peptide fragments [2]. Its physiological effect depends on pulsatile delivery; continuous exposure instead desensitises the receptor, which is the principle behind long-acting GnRH analogues such as leuprolide, goserelin and triptorelin used in prostate cancer, endometriosis and precocious puberty [1][18][15]. Peptides of this class are degraded in the gut, which is why oral delivery research is ongoing [19][20].

The identity of GnRH was settled by the groups of Andrew Schally and Roger Guillemin around 1971, and they shared the 1977 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on hypothalamic peptide hormones [15][1]. Gonadorelin was marketed for human diagnostic use as Factrel by 1978, and the pulsatile product Lutrepulse was studied in a multicenter trial reported in 1990 [2][3]. Wikipedia describes it as widely sold for veterinary use in many countries and as not available for clinical use in humans in the United States [2]. The TRT-forum use grew out of clinics offering it as an alternative when hCG was hard to obtain or poorly tolerated [5][21].

Forum users compare gonadorelin with hCG, which Wikipedia describes as the long-standing choice for supporting testicular function during TRT and which is also used by bodybuilders during and after anabolic steroid cycles [7]. hCG is a prescription drug in the US; Wikipedia notes shortages of injectable hCG linked to its weight-loss marketing, and cautions that prolonged use in men can raise androgen production and that it should be used very carefully in prepubescent teens because of the risk of premature growth-plate closure [7].

Others discuss clomiphene or low-dose hCG [22], and some rotate gonadorelin with kisspeptin-10 when hCG is not tolerated [21]. Kisspeptin is a peptide that triggers GnRH release; it has been tested in early trials for low sexual desire in men and women [16].

Users on TRT describe being prescribed gonadorelin in place of hCG to maintain testicular size and fertility [4][5][23]. One poster describes a prescription pairing testosterone with an aromatase inhibitor and gonadorelin instead of hCG [4]. Another lists gonadorelin among the peptides a clinic made available alongside testosterone and oxandrolone [24].

Reported experiences vary. Some users who switched from hCG describe continued atrophy or aching [5][6], citing the peptide's short half-life, while others use it with testosterone for fertility goals [14]. A user dealing with high estradiol on injections asks whether gonadorelin is part of others' regimens [25]. A user seeking information on gonadorelin acetate notes difficulty finding clear efficacy data [26]. These are anecdotes, not controlled data.

Clinical research on gonadorelin concerns reproductive medicine: pulsatile therapy in hypothalamic amenorrhea [3], hypogonadotropic hypogonadism [8][9][10], PCOS infertility [11], and neoadjuvant hormone treatment in infants with undescended testes, in which a randomized trial examined safety [27]. A pump-delivery pharmacokinetic study was withdrawn before enrolment [28]. No human trial identified has tested gonadorelin as an hCG substitute in men receiving testosterone, or for physique or appearance outcomes.

Pulsatile gonadorelin in the amenorrhea trial was reported to have a low rate of complications [3]. Safety in the self-directed TRT context has not been studied in published trials; forum users report injection-site and hormone-related side effects inconsistently [6][5]. Testosterone therapy itself carries documented risks that Wikipedia lists, including raised hematocrit, worsened sleep apnea and effects on spermatogenesis [17].

Legal status differs by country: Wikipedia lists it as prescription-only in Canada and not available for clinical use in humans in the US, while forum users describe it being prescribed by clinics alongside testosterone therapy [2][4][5].

lore.intro: Gonadorelin is discussed in TRT threads as an hCG alternative for preserving testicular function and fertility, with users split on whether it does the job [4][5][22].
